Deportment means the way a person carries themselves — both physically and behaviorally — especially in front of others.

Think of it as the overall impression your body, posture, movement, and conduct create when people look at you or interact with you. It is how you present yourself to the world.
It Has Two Closely Related Sides

The word covers two things that are deeply connected:

1. Physical deportment — how you hold and move your body.

This includes:

  • Your posture (do you stand straight or slouch?)
  • The way you walk (do you move gracefully or clumsily?)
  • The way you sit (do you sit properly or sprawl carelessly?)
  • Your gestures and overall bodily presence

A person with good physical deportment moves with confidence, grace, and control. They don't fidget, slump, or shuffle around. Think of a soldier standing at attention, or a professional dancer moving across a room — that is excellent physical deportment.

2. Behavioral deportment — how you conduct yourself in social situations.

This includes:

  • Your manners
  • Your tone and attitude toward others
  • Whether you behave appropriately for the occasion
  • Your overall social conduct

A person with good behavioral deportment is composed, polite, dignified, and appropriate in how they act. They know how to behave at a formal dinner, in a professional meeting, or during a serious conversation.
The Key Point: Both Sides Work Together

In practice, when people use the word deportment, they often mean both at once — the complete picture of how someone carries and conducts themselves. Your posture and your manner. Your body language and your behavior. Together, these things tell the world a lot about your upbringing, confidence, discipline, and character.

• "The young officer's deportment was impeccable — he stood tall, spoke calmly, and treated everyone with respect."
  • "Her deportment at the ceremony impressed everyone; she moved gracefully and conducted herself with quiet dignity."
  • "The teacher scolded him not for his grades, but for his poor deportment in class — slouching, interrupting others, and being disrespectful."

Deportment is a somewhat formal word. You won't hear it in casual everyday conversations very often. It tends to appear in:

  • Writing about etiquette, manners, or professionalism
  • Military or school contexts
  • Descriptions of someone's character or social polish
  • Literature, especially from earlier centuries

It is not a slang word, and it carries a sense of refinement and discipline. When someone praises another's deportment, it is a genuine compliment about their poise and self-presentation.

The word is most commonly used in the context of good deportment (praising someone), but it can describe bad deportment too.

  • Good deportment: graceful, upright, composed, dignified, controlled, poised
  • Poor/bad deportment: slouchy, rude, fidgety, undisciplined, inappropriate, sloppy in bearing or behavior
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Posture only refers to how you hold your body physically. Deportment is broader — it includes behavior too.
  • Manners only refers to social behavior and politeness. Deportment is broader — it includes the physical/bodily side too.
  • Conduct refers purely to behavior and actions. Deportment adds the layer of physical bearing and appearance of self-control.
  • Bearing is very close in meaning to deportment, but bearing leans more toward the physical (how you carry your body), while deportment more naturally covers both the physical and the social.

Deportment = the total way you carry yourself — in body AND behavior — especially in a way that reflects discipline, grace, and self-awareness.

If someone says you have excellent deportment, they mean: you stand well, move well, and conduct yourself well. You are composed, dignified, and polished. That is deportment.
